title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
tagline: The cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis: phases, significance and the differences between the two kinds of division.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Biology registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A cell does not divide at random; it passes through an orderly cycle of growth and division. This chapter describes the cell cycle, the phases of mitosis and the differences between mitosis and meiosis. Mitosis is the division that produces genetically similar daughter cells for growth and repair, while meiosis produces gametes with half the chromosome number. Understanding the sequence of events and their biological meaning is the main aim of the chapter.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Cell cycle; phases of mitosis; significance of mitosis; meiosis and its stages; differences between mitosis and meiosis

learningOutcomes: Describe the phases of the cell cycle.
Explain the main events of each phase of mitosis.
Describe the main events of meiosis.

blocks.text: The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its contents and divides. It includes a long preparation phase called interphase and a division phase called the M phase. Interphase itself has sub-phases in which the cell grows and duplicates its DNA. The cycle is regulated so that a cell does not divide until it is ready.

items: The cell cycle includes interphase and M phase.
Interphase has stages for growth and DNA replication.
M phase includes nuclear division and cytokinesis.
The cycle is regulated, not random.

items.text: A cell that has not yet replicated its DNA is in an early part of interphase, while a cell about to divide has already prepared its genetic material.
items.note: The cell cycle is more than just division; much of it is preparation.

blocks.text: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus that results in two daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. It is usually described in stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm. In prophase the chromosomes condense, in metaphase they align at the middle, in anaphase they separate, and in telophase the nuclei reform.

items: Mitosis produces two similar daughter nuclei.
Stages include prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Chromosomes align at the equator in metaphase.
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase.
Cytokinesis completes cell division.

items.text: During anaphase, the two chromatids of each chromosome separate and move to opposite poles, so that each future daughter cell will receive a complete set.
items.note: Mitosis is not about reducing chromosome number; it is about keeping it the same.

blocks.text: Mitosis is important for growth, repair and replacement of cells. Because the daughter cells are genetically similar to the parent cell, mitosis maintains the chromosome number and the genetic consistency of somatic cells. It is the kind of division that takes place in most body tissues during growth and healing.

items: Mitosis is used for growth and repair.
Daughter cells are genetically similar.
Chromosome number stays the same.
It is the usual division of somatic cells.

items.text: When skin is cut, mitosis helps replace the lost cells so the tissue can heal.
items.note: Mitosis is continuous in many tissues that need regular replacement.

blocks.text: Meiosis is a special type of division that produces gametes with half the chromosome number. It involves two successive divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II. In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair and then separate, so the chromosome number is reduced. In meiosis II, the chromatids separate, more like mitosis. The result is four haploid cells that are genetically different from each other in many cases.

items: Meiosis produces haploid gametes.
It involves two divisions.
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes.
Meiosis II separates chromatids.
Meiosis introduces genetic variation.

items.text: In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes come together and then move apart, so each resulting nucleus gets only one member of each homologous pair.
items.note: Meiosis I is where the chromosome number is halved.

blocks.text: Mitosis and meiosis have different functions and different outcomes. Mitosis maintains chromosome number and produces identical daughter cells, while meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces variation. Comparing them is useful because the differences highlight their different biological roles.

items: Mitosis: two daughter cells, same chromosome number.
Meiosis: four daughter cells, half the chromosome number.
Mitosis produces identical cells; meiosis produces variation.
Meiosis involves pairing and separation of homologous chromosomes.

items.text: Skin cell division is mitotic; formation of gametes is meiotic. The first maintains the body; the second is for reproduction.
items.note: The function of each division explains most of the differences.

keyPoints: The cell cycle includes interphase and M phase.
Mitosis has prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Mitosis produces two genetically similar daughter cells.
Meiosis involves two divisions and halves the chromosome number.
Mitosis is for growth and repair; meiosis is for gamete formation.
examFocus: When asked for the significance of mitosis, mention growth, repair and maintenance of chromosome number.
Do not confuse meiosis I and meiosis II; meiosis I is the division that reduces chromosome number.

vocabulary.meaning: The sequence of events by which a cell grows and divides.
Nuclear division producing two similar daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number.
A two-step division that halves the chromosome number to produce gametes.
Division of the cytoplasm following nuclear division.
Pairs of chromosomes with the same structure and genetic loci, one from each parent.

questions.prompt: The division of the cytoplasm following nuclear division is called:
questions.explanation: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it karyokinesis, which refers to nuclear division.

questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two genetically similar daughter cells.
questions.commonMistake: Saying meiosis and mitosis both produce four cells.

questions.prompt: In which stage of mitosis do chromosomes align at the equator?
questions.explanation: Chromosomes align at the equatorial plate in metaphase.

questions.prompt: Why is meiosis important for sexual reproduction?
questions.answer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce gametes and introduces genetic variation.
questions.explanation: Meiosis is important for maintaining chromosome number across generations and for variation.
questions.commonMistake: Saying meiosis only increases the number of cells.

questions.prompt: State two differences between mitosis and meiosis.
questions.answer: Mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number; meiosis produces four daughter cells with half the chromosome number. Mitosis gives genetically similar cells; meiosis produces variation.
questions.explanation: A good answer contrasts both the number of cells and the chromosome number or genetic outcome.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one difference when two are asked for.
